Tabatas are meant to be high intensity cardio. So, first of all, if you're doing them with something like pushups or situps, you're basically wasting your time. This is more akin to bodybuilding "pump" training than interval training, with high reps and low rest. So while you will likely get a nice pump from this, you're not improving your conditioning or resting heart rate one bit.

Another thing, tabatas [as done in the original study they're named after] are meant to be done at an insane level of intensity, 170% of VO2max. You, as a regular person, are unlikely to have a way to measure that. That's not necessarily a bad thing, nor should it serve as a deterrent to your doing HIIT, but know that it is supposed to be all-out effort, and that you're not likely able to reach it at your current fitness level even with that. The study was done with Olympic-level athletes, after all.

If you really want to build up to doing actual tabatas the way they were originally meant to be done, you could do 8, 20 seconds bursts of exercise with more than 10 seconds of rest inbetween, and gradually take it down to 10, while being careful to maintain the required level of intensity. It might take awhile, but it would eventually get you there.

Otherwise, if you just wanted to get into HIIT but don't care if your protocol is scientific and Japanese in origin, there are a whole mess of different interval training protocols you could play around with, from 30 seconds on/60 seconds off, to 60 seconds on/75 seconds off, or, my personal favorite because it doesn't require a timer or any other equipment, sprinting a distance, walking back and sprinting again.

The important thing to remember is that HIIT is supposed to be, well, high intensity, and you need to adjust your protocol based on how long it takes, so that you can keep it up the whole time and aren't moving at a snail's pace by the end. For example, tabatas can require ridiculous intensity because they only last four minutes, but if you were going to do 60 seconds on/75 seconds off for ten rounds, you would have to go a bit easier on yourself, because no one on Earth can keep up absolute intensity for that long of a training session.

Likewise, if you did "tabatas" but didn't actually keep up the mandated level of intensity, you would be getting a suboptimal workout.

You will also have to choose different protocols based on your current level of fitness and how much effort you can squeeze into a given period of time. So while if you're in extremely good shape, tabatas might let you get the same workload in in less time, someone who's not an elite athlete would need to spread the workload over a longer period of time at somewhat lower intensity, something like sprints/walkbacks.

So, that's the truth about tabatas and HIIT in general. TL;DR, most people couldn't do tabatas if they tried, so pick a different HIIT protocol that better suits your needs.
